meta.title: The Family Tree of Healing
meta.from: Transmission links extracted from the 15 fact-checked chapters in chapters/final/; duplicates merged.
meta.era_start: Approximate year (negative = BCE) of the earliest sourced appearance of the tradition in the written record, for layout only. null = no sourced date; place by edges. Indigenous traditions are far older than their first written record.
meta.certainty: Optional edge field: documented | debated | claimed | prestige-only. Legends are flagged in 'how'.

nodes.name: Persian medicine (Gondishapur)
nodes.era_label: 6th-8th c. CE (scale of the school debated)

nodes.name: Korean medicine (Hanui)
nodes.era_label: Chinese texts by 5th-6th c. CE; Dongui Bogam 1613; Sasang medicine 1894

nodes.name: Japanese medicine (Kampo)
nodes.era_label: Records cite 459 and 562 (some date arrival to 7th c.); Ishinpo 984

nodes.name: Islamic / Greco-Arabic medicine (Unani Tibb)

nodes.name: Tibetan medicine (Sowa Rigpa)
nodes.era_label: Dunhuang manuscripts before early 11th c.; Four Tantras usually dated 12th c.

nodes.name: Monte Cassino and the School of Salerno
nodes.era_label: From c. 800 (disputed); Constantine the African c. 1077

edges.how: Akkadian-speaking scholars took over, translated and expanded Sumerian medical and incantation texts, copied in scribal schools and healer families; Babylonian texts were later collected in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (7th c. BCE; sacked 612 BCE).

Overlapping regions and periods, contact through Asia Minor (Kos lies just offshore). Geller sees one Near Eastern medical system before Hippocrates; Asper sees transmission in the 9th-7th c. BCE; Vitas sees a shared tradition rather than direct borrowing.

edges.when: Up to about the 4th century CE (minority view on how long cuneiform stayed readable)
edges.how: Akkadian loanwords and translated recipes in Talmudic remedies, especially the Gittin collection, possibly via Aramaic translations.
Siddha's head-to-toe zodiac mapping of the body follows the Babylonian and Greco-Roman order rather than the Indian toe-to-head order.

edges.when: c. 8th century BCE (Homer) to 5th-4th century BCE (Hippocratic corpus)
edges.how: Literary reputation (Odyssey 4.229-230: Egypt a land rich in pharmaka) and 'Egyptian oil' remedies prescribed in Hippocratic gynaecological treatises.

edges.when: 6th century BCE (Cyrus and Amasis; Darius I)
edges.how: Cyrus requested Egypt's best eye-doctor from Amasis; Egyptian physicians kept at Darius's court (Herodotus 3.1, 3.129-130).

edges.when: After 331 BCE; Dioscorides 1st c. CE, Galen 2nd c. CE
edges.how: Conquest and Greek settlement; Egyptian ingredients and remedies (natron, alum, kuphi, achariston eye-salve, Isis plaster) entered Greek medical texts. Imhotep worshipped as Imouthes and identified with Asclepius (legend built on a historical person).
Prestige borrowing, not transmission: Greek physicians labelled their own compounds 'Egyptian' (e.g. Andromachos' Egyptian plaster, recorded by Galen).
Alexander's camp in the Indus region used Indian healers for snakebite (Nearchus via Arrian, Indica 15; Strabo XV.1.45). Contact and practical use, not a transfer of theory.

Asclepieia modeled on Epidaurus spread across the classical world; after Roman conquest, Greek-speaking physicians served Rome (Dioscorides with Nero's armies; Galen at the courts of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus).
Oribasius, Aetius and Paul of Aegina condensed Galen into handbooks; illustrated Dioscorides copied in Constantinople for Anicia Juliana.
Abbasid translation movement in Baghdad: Greek to Syriac to Arabic, led by Hunayn ibn Ishaq (c. 808/809-873) with his son Ishaq and nephew Hubaysh.
Galen's commentaries on the Hippocratic On the Nature of Man made humoral theory dominant in European medicine until the Scientific Revolution.

edges.when: 1st century CE to end of 15th century; Leechbook c. 950; Hildegard 12th c.
edges.how: Copied manuscripts of Dioscorides served as Europe's primary pharmacology text; monastic Latin texts adapted alongside native English remedies in Bald's Leechbook; Hildegard's works reflect classical theory.

edges.when: 8th-12th centuries (indirect); 'Galenos at court' legend first recorded 16th c.
edges.how: Indirect traces through western and Persian intermediaries, mainly in urine diagnosis; secondary to Indian and Chinese inputs. The Galenos story is legend.
The Bower Manuscript, Sanskrit medical texts on birch bark found near Kucha; the Navanitaka quotes Charaka's formulas.

edges.when: First millennium CE, visible in Tang-era texts (7th c.)
edges.how: Buddhist routes from India and Central Asia (and on to Korea and East Asia); Sun Simiao's Qianjin yaofang and Qianjin yifang include prescriptions linked to Jivaka, the Indian 'Medicine King'.

edges.when: c. 8th-12th centuries CE; Four Tantras usually dated 12th c.
edges.how: Buddhist transmission and translation of Indian medical works; Vagbhata's Ashtanga Hridaya forms the main body of the Four Tantras.
The Fifth Dalai Lama brought the Indian physician Manaho, skilled in cataract surgery, to his court.

edges.when: c. 800 CE (Barmakid patronage, before 803) to c. 850 (al-Tabari); still used by al-Biruni, early 11th c.
edges.how: Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas translated (often via Persian) into Arabic in Baghdad; Indian physicians such as Manka named (details contested). Al-Tabari's Firdaws al-Hikma has a 36-part section on Indian medicine drawing on Sushruta, Charaka and Madhava.
Shared Sanskrit-Tamil learned culture; Siddha adopted Ayurveda's five elements, three humours, seven tissues and vital winds.
Tamil revivalism, the Dravidian movement and colonial committees led Tamil physicians to define Siddha as distinct from Ayurveda ('Ayulvetam').
Garcia de Orta's Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India, written in Portuguese Goa.

An Indian practitioner rebuilt Cowasjee's nose with a forehead flap; reported in the Madras Gazette (Aug 1794) and the Gentleman's Magazine (Oct 1794, 'B. L.'). Carpue operated 22 Oct 1814 and published 1816; von Graefe coined 'plastic surgery'.

edges.when: Pali canon onward; date of Tamil version unknown
edges.how: The Jivaka skull-opening healer story spread through Buddhist literature (Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese) and resembles the Agastya/Theraiyar skull legend. Legend.
Pulse diagnosis and urine examination 'in all probability' derived from Unani via Arabic and Persian medicine in India.
Siddha author Iramatevar travelled to Mecca, studied, converted to Islam and took the name Yakkopu.

edges.when: Diploma from 1929 (Colombo); University of Jaffna 1984; Faculty gazetted 2024
edges.how: Tamil communities and formal indigenous-medicine education.

edges.when: Before the early 11th century (Dunhuang) and in the 12th-century Four Tantras
edges.how: Pulse diagnosis and moxibustion; three of the few Tibetan medical manuscripts at Dunhuang deal with moxibustion.
Musk trade routes; loanwords for theriac, camphor and saffron at Dunhuang; urine analysis in the Medical Method of the Lunar King closely resembles Ibn Sina's Canon.

edges.when: From the 17th century; colleges 1662-1937; revival after 1990
edges.how: Institutionalized with the Gelug monastic order; more than 100 monastery medical colleges (manba datsan).
Monastery medical schools modeled on Labrang; copies of the Lhasa medical paintings (an early 20th-century set survives in Ulan-Ude).
Tibetan refugee institutions in exile; Central Council for Indian Medicine (Amendment) Act 2010.

edges.when: By the 5th-6th century CE; classics such as the Shanghan lun in the Tang-Song period
edges.how: Medical texts and physicians moving along diplomatic and Buddhist routes; Korea acted as the bridge eastward.
I Ching nomenclature and Neo-Confucian ethics shaped Yi Je-ma's Sasang constitutional medicine (Dongui Suse Bowon).

edges.when: 5th-6th century CE (records cite 459 and 562; some accounts date it to the 7th c.)
edges.how: Korean physicians and Chinese medical books carried across the Korea Strait, partly by Buddhist monks.
Tamba Yasuyori compiled the 30-volume Ishinpo from Chinese medical texts, preserving many later lost in China.
Transmission of classic texts such as the Shanghan lun.
Tashiro Sanki studied in China about 12 years and brought Jin-Yuan theory home (Gosei-ha school).
China's Shanghan lun revival inspired Japan's Koho-ha school; Yoshimasu Todo built pattern-to-formula diagnosis and abdominal palpation.
edges.source: Nihon Toyo Igaku Zasshi abstract ; Watanabe et al. 2011, PMC3114407

edges.how: Accounts of Hua Tuo's lost mafeisan inspired Hanaoka Seishu's mafutsusan herbal anaesthetic (Hua Tuo's formula itself is lost).
edges.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanaoka_Seish%C5%AB ; Anesthesiology 'Balanced Anesthesia with Moonflowers and Monkshoods'

edges.how: Dongui Bogam (1613) reprinted and translated in Japan.
Dongui Bogam reprinted more than 30 times in China (and translated in Vietnam).
Rangaku (Dutch learning) via Nagasaki; translation of a Dutch version of Kulmus's anatomy.
edges.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaitai_Shinsho ; National Diet Library Japan-Netherlands exchange pages

edges.how: Hanaoka's operation under herbal general anaesthesia on Kan Aiya, 42 years before Morton's 1846 ether demonstration.
Meiji government required all physicians to study Western medicine; Kampo declined but was not banned.
Regional spread and integration into health systems.
Acupuncture and moxibustion spread internationally through master-disciple lines and academic education.
Nkrumah sent Dr. Oku Ampofo to China to study herbal medicine.

edges.when: Ge Hong 4th c. CE; artemisinin early 1970s; Nobel 2015
edges.how: Tu Youyou reread Ge Hong's Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies on qinghao, switched to low-temperature extraction and isolated artemisinin.

edges.when: 6th-8th century CE; Jibrail ibn Bukhtishu invited to Baghdad under Harun al-Rashid (r. 786-809)
edges.how: Gondishapur-trained physician families (Bukhtishu) brought the hospital model and Greek-Persian learning to Baghdad; first Baghdad bimaristan. Some historians think later accounts enlarged the school.
Al-Zahrawi in Cordoba built his surgical treatise partly on Paul of Aegina's work.
Salerno's port linked Italy with North Africa, Greece and the Middle East; manuscripts gathered and translated at Monte Cassino.

edges.when: Late 11th century (Constantine the African at Monte Cassino c. 1077; d. 1087)
edges.how: Latin translation of al-Majusi's Royal Book (Pantegni) and the Viaticum, feeding the School of Salerno and early universities.

edges.when: From c. 1100; Canon translated 12th c., taught until mid-17th c.; printed 1470s
edges.how: Second wave of Arabic-to-Latin translation in Spain, especially Toledo (Gerard of Cremona's Canon of Ibn Sina); Hunayn's Isagoge in Latin became the nucleus of the Articella; al-Zahrawi's illustrated surgery (about 200 instruments) translated into Latin.
Latin and other European translations and printed editions of al-Razi's treatise on smallpox and measles.

edges.when: Medieval period onward; Tibbi Conference 1906; Department of AYUSH 2003
edges.how: Hakims settling in the subcontinent; Ayurvedic and Unani Tibbia College in Delhi teaching both systems.
Arabic-language manuscript scholarship along trans-Saharan networks (Timbuktu libraries).

edges.when: Late 9th century (claimed in a gloss in a c. 950 manuscript)
edges.how: Remedies said to have been sent to Alfred the Great; recorded in Leechbook II ch. 64. Claim, not verified.
Bock and Dodoens copied Fuchs's woodcuts; Dodoens translated into English by Lyte and reworked by Gerard (commissioned by John Norton).
A reprint of Culpeper's herbal reportedly the first medical book printed in North America.
Withering names Fuchs as the first to describe foxglove.

edges.when: Recipe 1775; An Account of the Foxglove 1785
edges.how: Withering identified foxglove among about twenty herbs in a Shropshire family dropsy recipe and tested it in 156 cases (digitalis). The 'Mother Hutton' story is undocumented.
Edward Stone's willow-bark report to the Royal Society; Buchner named salicin; Bayer chemists synthesised acetylsalicylic acid.
Apothecary's assistant Friedrich Serturner isolated morphine from opium, the first plant alkaloid isolated; Jenner built vaccination (1796) on the older variolation tradition.

edges.when: Chinese records from c. mid-1500s; exact origin unknown
edges.how: Variolation spread along trade routes; origin agreed to be in Asia (China or India); early Indian claims disputed.
Variolation spread along trade routes into Africa and the Middle East.
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu observed inoculation in Constantinople and promoted it in England, including at court.
Onesimus, an enslaved man inoculated as a child in West Africa, told Cotton Mather; Mather and Zabdiel Boylston promoted inoculation.

edges.when: Era of the Atlantic slave trade onward
edges.how: Forced migration of Yoruba people to the Americas carried healing and plant knowledge.

edges.when: Jesuits learned of the bark c. 1620-1630; in Jesuit colleges from 1650; Talbor late 1600s
edges.how: Jesuit missionaries in Peru carried cinchona ('Jesuit's powder', 'Peruvian bark') to Europe.
Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine from cinchona bark in Paris.

edges.when: Dutch 1852; British (Markham) 1860; Ootacamund 1861; Ledger/Manuel Mamani seeds 1865
edges.how: Seed-collecting expeditions and smuggling for colonial plantations.
Fusion of native and Christian religious traditions in Kallawaya healing.
Hahnemann's translation of William Cullen's Materia Medica and his cinchona self-experiment (Andean bark via European materia medica).

Martin de la Cruz's herbal translated into Latin by Juan Badiano at Tlatelolco (returned to Mexico 1990); Philip II's physician Francisco Hernandez surveyed New Spain's plants; Sahagun's Florentine Codex recorded Tlatelolco healers' plant knowledge.

edges.when: Reports 1516 and 1590s; Bernard 1846; tubocurarine 1935; Montreal 23 Jan 1942
edges.how: Explorers' reports and samples of curare arrow poison, laboratory research, then clinical use as a surgical muscle relaxant.
Richard Evans Schultes's fieldwork in Colombia, learning from Indigenous healers such as Salvador Chindoy (20th-century ethnobotany).
Patent-medicine seller H.C.F. Meyer sold echinacea and sent it to Eclectic physician John King.

edges.when: Kolb 1719; Britain c. 1815; Germany c. 1825; Dublin Pharmacopoeia 1826
edges.how: Cape colonial contact and travellers' records, then export trade in dried buchu leaves.

edges.when: US Dispensatory 1833; USP 1842; Helmbold's Extract 1846; dropped from USP 1930
edges.how: Buchu export trade from the Cape to the United States, including patent medicines.
Rooibos recorded by a botanical traveller, then immigrant trade and settler cultivation.
An anthropologist's publication on San use of Hoodia was read by government scientists, then patented and licensed (Phytopharm, Pfizer, Unilever).

edges.when: Hoodia agreement 24 March 2003; rooibos agreement 25 May 2019, first payout 2022
edges.how: Access and benefit-sharing agreements (Biodiversity Act, Nagoya Protocol; 1.5% rooibos farm-gate levy).
Periwinkle tea used in Jamaica; leaves sent to the University of Western Ontario, where Noble, Beer and Cutts isolated vinblastine.

edges.when: Polynesian settlement of Hawaiʻi (centuries before 1778; dates debated)
edges.how: Canoe plants (ʻawa, noni, kukui, ʻōlena) carried by voyaging canoes.
Missionary suppression; licensing that required Western botanical names.
University of Hawaiʻi medical school cultural competence courses (1990) and Department of Native Hawaiian Health (2003); integrated clinics.
Legal suppression, then Ministry of Health standards (1999) and a rongoā development plan (2006).
Traditional tea-tree leaf use preceded A.R. Penfold's antiseptic studies at Sydney's Technological Museum, launching the commercial industry.
First Fleet surgeon Denis Considen sent Sydney peppermint (eucalyptus) oil to Joseph Banks.
Benedict Lust bought the rights to the term 'naturopathy' from homeopathic physician John H. Scheel.
Lust, treated by Father Kneipp, returned to the US as his representative, founded Kneipp Societies, then the American School of Naturopathy (1901).
D.D. Palmer practised as a magnetic healer before the Lillard adjustment in Davenport, Iowa.
A.T. Still styled himself 'the Lightning Bone Setter' from 1874.
The Flexner Report (Carnegie Foundation) made the Johns Hopkins scientific model the standard; about one-third of schools, including many sectarian and proprietary ones, closed.
